text: The Quiet Corner before you has witnessed some of the darkest days in Greyfriars history. In the 17th century, King Charles I introduced reforms that sparked a religious civil war and that would last decades. He tried to force the heavily Presbyterian Church of Scotland to adopt his high church practices that would bring the Scottish church in line with the Church of England and introduce a new book of common prayer in 1637 which caused widespread outrage. Many Scots saw this as an attack on their faith and freedoms and as suspiciously pro-Catholic due to his marriage to Henrietta Maria, a Roman Catholic French princess. In 1638 thousands of Presbyterians joined together in protest and signed the National Covenant, right here in Greyfriars itself, the original document on display within the Greyfriars Museum. We all and every one of us under written do protest that after long and due examination of our own conscience in matters of true and false religion, we are now thoroughly resolved of the truth by the word and spirit of God and therefore we believe with our hearts confess with our mouths, subscribe with our hands and constantly affirm before God and the whole world that this is the only true Christian faith and religion. The National Covenant pledged to defend the independence of the Scottish kirk, kirk being an Old Scots word for church. Their defiance would plunge Scotland into decades of religious civil war. While initially successful in their crusade against the Crown's enforcement of new religious law during the many battles fought between the Crown and the Covenanters, their success waned after Cromwell's invasion of Scotland and the reformation of the Crown. The Covenanters experienced a crushing defeat at the Battle of Bothwell Bridge in 1679 and around 1,200 captured Covenanters were marched to Edinburgh and imprisoned here, beside Greyfriars Kirkyard. The prisoners held here were not kept in cells but in an open enclosure with walls surrounding the rough field leaving little to no protection from the elements. For months they were left exposed to the harsh Scottish weather, many of the prisoners were wounded, exhausted and already weakened from their defeat at the Battle of Bothwell Bridge. Food was scarce and disease spread rampant through the crowded camp due to the filthy conditions. With no real shelter the prisoners endured freezing nights, hunger, disease and constant. This was truly a place where hope, the conditions were so poor that it is often referred to as the world's first concentration camp. Another one gone in the night, just lying there when the sun came up. The rain won't stop, it never stops. They want us to sign it, to renounce the covenant. I won't sign it, I won't renounce my faith, not for them, not for anyone. Last chance, sign your hand. Some were offered the opportunity to leave if they embraced the King's beliefs, but they refused. Many died from the brutal conditions, others were executed or transported across the Atlantic as indentured labourers, never to see Scotland again. The suffering endured within these walls has given rise to countless legends. For generations visitors have spoken of an overwhelming sense of unease, as though unseen eyes were following their every step. Others describe sudden chills or temperature drops, shadowy figures moving between the tombstones or the faint sound of voices carried on the wind. In 2014 a woman even fell unconscious when touring the Covenanters prison and when she awoke she found bruises around her neck. Whether these stories are a product of imagination, the power of suggestion or something far more mysterious is impossible to say. But few leave this corner of Greyfriars without feeling that its tragic past has somehow. Whenever you're ready to continue the chapter, please go to the next stop on the map.
